items.stem: ‘Germany was mainly responsible for the outbreak of war in 1914.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: The blank cheque encouraged Austria to take a hard line. German war plans required an attack on France through Belgium. German leaders believed a war sooner was better than later. Against: Austria-Hungary decided on war against Serbia for its own reasons. Russia's general mobilisation turned a local war into a European one. items.answer: For: Austria-Hungary chose war against Serbia. Russia's early mobilisation escalated the crisis. France backed Russia; Serbian nationalists began the crisis. items.stem: How far do intentionalist and structural approaches to the origins of the war complement each other?
items.answer: For: Structures limited the choices leaders felt they had. Leaders' intentions were shaped by structures such as alliances. Most modern accounts combine both. Against: They lead to different judgements about responsibility. Intentionalists blame particular governments; structuralists blame the system. They rely on different kinds of evidence. Judgement: the approaches are complementary in explaining how war came, but they lead to different judgements on who was responsible.

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 1965 (illustrative). “The memoranda of the Kaiser's ministers reveal a single thread. Again and again they speak of breaking the ring of enemies, of a place in the sun, of the need to strike before Russia grows too strong. These were not idle words; they guided the decisions of July 1914.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: German leaders intended to break out of encirclement by war, and these intentions guided their decisions in July 1914. Approach: An intentionalist approach that uses the private statements and documents of German leaders to reveal their intentions. Own knowledge that supports it: Moltke and others argued for war before Russian rearmament was complete. Weltpolitik sought a "place in the sun". The blank cheque reflected a willingness to risk war. Own knowledge that challenges it: Statements of intent do not prove a plan was followed. Other powers' decisions also mattered. Leaders also feared war and tried to restrain Austria late in the crisis.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): demonstrates a full understanding of the historian's interpretation and approach, explained with close reference to the extract and tested against accurate own knowledge. Level 4 (13-16): explains the main interpretation with support from the extract and shows some understanding of the approach. Level 3 (9-12): identifies the main interpretation with some support, or explains sub-messages. Level 2 (5-8): identifies sub-messages or makes valid points about the topic linked to the extract. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases or summarises the extract, or writes about the topic without reference to it. (The examination question is marked out of 40; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: Study the extract. “The memoranda of the Kaiser's ministers reveal a single thread. Again and again they speak of breaking the ring of enemies, of a place in the sun, of the need to strike before Russia grows too strong. These were not idle words; they guided the decisions of July 1914.” (A historian writing in 1965 (illustrative).) Use your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain how far the evidence supports the interpretation in the extract.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Moltke and others argued for war before Russian rearmament was complete. Weltpolitik sought a "place in the sun". The blank cheque reflected a willingness to risk war. Challenging evidence: Statements of intent do not prove a plan was followed. Other powers' decisions also mattered. Leaders also feared war and tried to restrain Austria late in the crisis. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]

items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in 1969 (illustrative). “Once the railway timetables began to roll, nothing could stop them. The generals of every great power had planned for a war of rapid mobilisation, and mobilisation meant war. The statesmen of July 1914 found that the machines they had built had taken the decision out of their hands.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: War came because rigid mobilisation plans and railway timetables left statesmen no room to manoeuvre. Approach: A structural approach that explains the war through military planning and technology rather than the aims of individuals. Own knowledge that supports it: The Schlieffen Plan required an attack on France as soon as Russia mobilised. Russia could not partially mobilise against Austria alone. Railway timetables made mobilisation hard to stop. Own knowledge that challenges it: Statesmen chose to mobilise; the plans did not act by themselves. The Kaiser briefly considered halting the attack in the west on 1 August. Diplomacy continued until the last days.

items.stem: Analyse the reasons why the Fischer thesis caused such controversy in the 1960s.
items.answer: It overturned the post-war West German consensus that the powers had slid into war together. It implied continuity of aims from the Kaiser to Hitler. It relied on documents that critics argued were read selectively. It reopened the question of war guilt settled by Article 231. Judgement: its claim of continuity with Nazi aims touched the most sensitive issue in post-war German identity.

items.stem: Study the extract. “The documents of the German government leave little room for doubt. From the meeting of December 1912 to the war aims of September 1914, Germany's leaders pursued one aim: to break out of encirclement and establish German mastery in Europe. The blank cheque was not a blunder but a calculated risk, taken in the knowledge that it would probably bring a continental war.” (A historian writing in the 1960s (illustrative).) What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: Germany's leaders deliberately risked a European war in 1914 to achieve a long-standing aim of dominating Europe. Approach: The historian relies on German government documents and focuses on the aims and decisions of German leaders, tracing continuity from before the war into its war aims. Own knowledge that supports it: The blank cheque of 5-6 July 1914 promised Austria unconditional support. German leaders urged Vienna to act quickly against Serbia. The September Programme set out annexationist aims. Own knowledge that challenges it: The September Programme was drawn up after war began, so it may not show pre-war aims. The 1912 meeting led to no immediate decisions. Austria-Hungary and Russia also took decisions that escalated the crisis. Context: Fischer's work, using German archives, challenged the post-1945 West German consensus that all the powers had slid into war, and it provoked a fierce national controversy.

items.answer: Interpretation: Responsibility was shared among the powers, whose leaders blundered into a war none of them fully intended. Approach: The historian examines decision-making in several capitals during the July Crisis, stressing perceptions and contingency rather than a single plan. Own knowledge that supports it: Austria's ultimatum was designed to be rejected. Russia's general mobilisation on 30 July made war much more likely. France gave Russia firm support during Poincaré's visit in July. Own knowledge that challenges it: Germany's blank cheque encouraged Austria. German war plans turned a Balkan war into a European one. Fischer's evidence of German aims. Context: Written after the end of the Cold War, when archives in several capitals had been studied, this view moved away from the German-centred debate of the 1960s.

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in the 1960s (illustrative). “The war of 1914 was a war for the redivision of the world. Finance capital in Britain, Germany and France had outgrown its national markets; colonies, spheres of investment and sources of raw materials were the stakes. Governments managed this competition, and the workers of every nation were sent to die for it.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the First World War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: The war resulted from competition between capitalist imperialist powers for markets, investment and colonies. Approach: An economic approach that explains the war through capitalist interests and class, following Lenin's theory of imperialism. Own knowledge that supports it: Imperial rivalry in Africa and the Moroccan crises. Anglo-German trade competition. The Berlin-Baghdad railway alarmed Britain and Russia. Own knowledge that challenges it: Britain and Germany were major trading partners and many bankers opposed war. The crisis began in the Balkans, not over colonies. Imperial disputes such as Fashoda were settled peacefully. Context: Marxist interpretations followed Lenin's Imperialism (1916) and were the official view in the USSR and East Germany during the Cold War.
